title: First weeks in the programme: what I expected and what surprised me
excerpt: I arrived expecting to learn mostly about technology. A few weeks in, the bigger lesson is that energy questions are really questions about people, institutions and trade-offs.
body:
I've been meaning to start this journal since orientation, and I'm finally sitting down to write. Part of the reason for keeping it public is accountability — if I write things down where others can see them, I'm more likely to keep going.

## What I expected

I came into the Master of Sustainability expecting energy security to be mostly about supply: pipelines, power plants, reserves and the occasional geopolitical crisis. I assumed I'd spend most of my time learning the technical side of renewables and how grids work.

## What surprised me

The technical material is there, but what's struck me most so far is how *interdisciplinary* every conversation becomes. A discussion about a new transmission line turns out to be about land, treaty rights, consultation, prices, jobs and the climate — all at once. My classmates come from very different backgrounds, and I've already learned as much from their questions as from the readings.

I've also had to get comfortable with uncertainty. Many of the questions we're asked don't have a single correct answer. They have better and worse arguments, and the work is in explaining the trade-offs clearly.

## Things I'm going to try

- Writing one short reflection a week, even if it's rough.
- Keeping a reading log with a one-line summary of each source.
- Asking "secure for whom?" whenever I read about energy security.
- Being braver about sharing half-formed ideas — like this post.

## Key takeaways

> Energy questions are rarely only technical. The interesting part is usually in the trade-offs, and in who gets to decide.
